common_name: Kinnow Mandarin (King x Willowleaf Hybrid Tangerine)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after the last frost danger has passed, once soil has warmed.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring after the last frost danger has passed, choosing a well-drained site with at least eight hours of direct sun and protection from cold winds. Water deeply and regularly during establishment, then taper to consistent moisture during fruit development while avoiding standing water. This vigorous mandarin hybrid produces deep orange, intensely sweet-tart fruit with numerous seeds and a tight peel, ripening in mid to late winter. It tolerates brief dips into the high 20s F once established but performs best where winters stay mild, making it a favorite in low-desert and Gulf Coast citrus plantings.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring once the danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring once the danger of frost has passed, siting them in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and room for a moderately vigorous canopy. Provide steady irrigation through bloom and fruit set, and fertilize with a balanced citrus formula during the growing season. Nova produces deep orange, easy-peeling fruit with a rich, honeyed flavor that ripens early in the mandarin season, though a pollinator variety nearby improves fruit set and reduces seediness. It suits home orchards across Florida, the Gulf Coast, and coastal California where winters stay above the low 20s F.

planting.note: Plant nursery trees in spring after frost risk passes, in a sunny, sheltered location.

directions: Plant nursery trees in spring after frost risk passes, in a sunny, sheltered location with well-drained soil enriched with organic matter. Keep the root zone evenly moist during establishment and reduce watering slightly as fruit begins to color to concentrate sugars. Robinson bears loose-skinned, richly flavored orange fruit that ripens earlier than most mandarins, often by early fall, but it tends toward seediness unless grown in isolation from other citrus. It is popular with Florida and Gulf Coast home growers for its dependable early harvest and moderate cold tolerance.

common_name: Tarocco Blood Orange (Italian Half-Blood Sweet Orange)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above freezing.

directions: Plant grafted trees in spring once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above freezing, in full sun with deep, well-drained soil. Water deeply and consistently through the growing season, and expect the best red pigmentation where winter nights are cool but frost-free, as in coastal and inland California valleys. Tarocco fruit is nearly seedless with tender, aromatic flesh streaked or fully blushed red-purple and a flavor prized for its balance of sweetness and berry-like tang. It is considered the finest-flavored of the widely grown blood oranges but is more cold-sensitive than standard sweet oranges.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger has passed, in a warm, sunny site.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger has passed, in a warm, sunny site with well-drained soil, since this cultivar was selected for reliable fruiting in low-heat, low-humidity climates. Water regularly during establishment and reduce slightly as fruit matures to help concentrate flavor. Trovita produces medium-sized, thin-skinned oranges with juicy, sweet flesh and fewer seeds than many Valencia-type oranges, ripening in winter to early spring. Originating as a Washington Navel sport bred for desert and coastal Southern California conditions, it remains a dependable choice where summer heat is moderate.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after the last frost, in a sheltered, sunny spot.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring after the last frost, in a sheltered, sunny spot, since this cultivar can be shy-bearing in cooler coastal fog belts and benefits from reflected heat. Keep soil evenly moist and feed with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season to support its dense, spreading canopy. Kara fruit ripens late, often improving in flavor if left on the tree into late winter, developing a rich, aromatic sweetness with a soft, slightly fragile peel. It is a favorite among California backyard growers for its dessert-quality flavor, though it ships poorly and is rarely found in stores.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring once frost danger has passed, in full sun with well-drained soil.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring once frost danger has passed, in full sun with well-drained soil, as this compact selection stays smaller and denser than standard Nagami kumquat. Water deeply during dry spells and mulch to keep roots cool and moist through summer heat. Nordmann bears an abundance of small, oval, orange fruit with sweet edible skin and tart flesh, and unlike standard Nagami it produces few to no seeds, making it easier to eat out of hand. It is among the more cold-hardy true citrus types, tolerating brief drops into the upper teens F once mature, and is popular for Gulf Coast and lower Southeast gardens.

common_name: Bonnie Brae Lemon (California Heirloom Slender Lemon)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost risk has passed, in a warm, well-drained, sunny site.

directions: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost risk has passed, in a warm, well-drained, sunny site, giving this vigorous, somewhat thorny tree room to spread. Water consistently during establishment and avoid waterlogged soil, which quickly stresses lemon roots. Bonnie Brae produces distinctively long, slender, thin-skinned lemons with abundant tart juice and few seeds, and it can flower and fruit nearly year-round in mild climates. Once grown commercially in Southern California, it remains a sought-after heirloom for home growers who prize its exceptionally juicy fruit over its irregular, less market-friendly shape.

planting.note: Plant nursery trees in spring once frost danger has passed, in full sun with fertile, well-drained soil.

directions: Plant nursery trees in spring once frost danger has passed, in full sun with fertile, well-drained soil, allowing space for a nearly thornless, densely foliaged canopy. Provide even moisture throughout the year and protect young trees from hard freezes with covers or trunk wraps. Villafranca bears Eureka-type lemons that are medium-sized, juicy, and nearly seedless, produced almost continuously in warm climates with a heavier main crop in winter. Long grown in Florida and the Gulf Coast as a dooryard favorite, it is valued for producing well even under humid, subtropical conditions that can trouble other lemon cultivars.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger passes, in a sunny, sheltered location.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger passes, in a sunny, sheltered location with well-drained soil, since this older California cultivar performs best with reliable summer heat. Water deeply and regularly, and thin heavy fruit set to reduce the tree's tendency toward alternate bearing. Wilking produces deep orange, richly flavored fruit with a loose peel late in the mandarin season, and its flowers are notably fragrant. Though largely superseded commercially, it survives in heritage collections and backyard orchards as a parent of several modern mandarin hybrids, including Kinnow.
